title: Complexity, Data Structures and OOP
oneLiner: Pick algorithms that scale, store data in the structure that fits the job, and organise agents as objects.

what.html:
Time complexity (Big O) describes how much slower code gets as data grows. Data structures (lists, tuples, dictionaries, NumPy arrays, DataFrames) each suit different jobs. Object-oriented programming organises code into classes and objects, which maps neatly onto AI agents.

Everyday versionFinding a word by reading a dictionary page by page is O(n); opening it in the middle and halving each time is O(log n); a numbered locker you open directly is O(1).

why.html:
• With millions of rows, an O(n²) step can take days while O(n log n) takes seconds.
  • The wrong structure (searching a list instead of a dict) silently makes code thousands of times slower.
  • Clear classes make multi-agent systems easier to extend and test.

how.title: Big O: how work grows
how.html: O(1): same time whatever the size (look up by ID). O(log n): halve each step (binary search). O(n): touch each item once. O(n log n): good sorting. O(n²): compare every pair. O(n!): try every ordering, hopeless beyond tiny n.

how.title: Logarithms = halving
how.html: log₂ n is how many times you can halve n before reaching 1. A million items need only 20 halvings; a billion need 30. That's why binary search is so fast.

how.title: Lists, tuples and dictionaries
how.html: A list is a growable sequence you can change. A tuple is a fixed record you can't change (like a shape (224, 224, 3)). A dictionary maps keys to values and finds any key almost instantly, whatever its size. All three fetch an item by position or key in about the same time at any size.

how.title: NumPy and pandas
how.html: A NumPy array holds numbers of one type packed together, so whole-array maths runs in fast compiled code, roughly 100× faster than a Python loop. A DataFrame is a labelled table (columns can differ in type) for loading, cleaning, filtering and grouping data.

how.title: Pick the right one
how.html: CSV and cleaning → DataFrame. Feature names → list. Name-to-index map or hyperparameters → dict. Training matrix and weights → NumPy array. Shapes and image sizes → tuple.

how.title: Classes, inheritance, polymorphism
how.html: A class is a blueprint (Dog), an object is one instance (Tommy). Inheritance lets a new class reuse an old one (single, multilevel, hierarchical, multiple, hybrid). Polymorphism means the same method call behaves differently depending on the object.

how.title: Agents as objects
how.html: A base Agent class defines how to call the LLM; a ValidationAgent and SummaryAgent each override execute(); a workflow object holds both and calls execute() on each. Simple helpers like read_paper() stay plain functions.

demo.html: Step through how each object-oriented idea (class, object, inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation, abstraction, composition) shows up in a research-paper agent workflow.

example.html:
Customer deduplication. A team compares every customer with every other to find duplicates: O(n²). At 2 million customers that is 4 × 10¹² comparisons, which would take days. Grouping customers by a dictionary key (normalised email) first makes it O(n): one pass, each lookup O(1). Feature names live in a list, the name-to-column map in a dict, the numeric matrix in a NumPy array, and the raw data in a DataFrame.

Supplementary x in my_list scans the whole list; x in my_set is O(1) on average. Inside a loop this difference is the gap between seconds and hours.

misunderstandings: Big O tells you the exact running time.
It describes growth; constants and hardware still matter.
Indexing lists, tuples, dicts and arrays is O(1).
Single-element access can be slower; the win is whole-array operations.
Inheritance is always the best way to reuse code.
Composition (has-a) is often simpler and more flexible.
takeaways: Big O describes growth with n (and d in ML): O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n²) < O(n!).
log₂ n = halvings to 1; a million items need ~20 steps.
list: dynamic; tuple: fixed; dict: O(1) lookup; NumPy: vectorised maths; DataFrame: labelled tables.
Inheritance reuses code; polymorphism lets one call behave per type.
Agent systems: class = agent type, object = running agent, composition = multi-agent workflow.
thirty: Time complexity describes how running time grows with input size, written in Big O; in ML that means samples n and features d. Common classes are O(1) lookups, O(log n) binary search, where log₂ n counts the halvings, so a million items need about 20 steps, O(n) scans, O(n log n) sorting, O(n²) pairwise comparison and O(n!) brute force. For data structures, lists are dynamic arrays of references, tuples are immutable records, dictionaries are hash tables with O(1) average lookup, NumPy arrays are homogeneous and vectorised, about 100× faster than loops, and DataFrames are labelled tables for cleaning and analysis. In OOP, classes define agents, objects are running agents, inheritance creates specialists, polymorphism lets execute() vary by role, and composition builds multi-agent workflows.
